items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: Back then, he and Lee were very good buddies

ctx.x: Who else was on that date?

Ernie Henry -- on the side I was on, I think a pianist named Al Knight, and I think he had Arthur Taylor on the drums. On that side, I mean, on that record that Jazz by Gee they called it, I think. And Frank Foster and some others on the other side.

But that was the first thing I did for Riverside. And as I started playing around New York out in Brooklyn ... Kenny Dorham, Ernie Henry, people like that -- word of mouth gets around, you know, and like when you work, everybody starts calling you.

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: Lee Morgan Marvin, that's where he died at -- playing and when he'd get off the stand, they'd turn on the jukebox

ctx.x: Well, in the '50s, I notice even myself, in the '50s, when we were coming up, rock and roll was getting to be a thing that was being pushed, but you could still walk in the clubs and hear Billie Holiday or Charlie Parker on the jukebox. It was still available to you, even though rock and roll was being pushed more and more.

Well, let me tell you about that now. There are clubs -- just like Slugs -- they playing all that -- you know, when it was open -- playing all that good music in there -- Lee Morgan Marvin, that's where he died at -- playing and when he'd get off the stand, they'd turn on the jukebox and they got all this rock music on. That was a musician that would get off the bandstand and have earplugs in their ears or they'd have to go outside, because they can't stand to hear

the music. That's a heck of a contrast, you know. But that's the way it does. You hear that on the radio all day long. All you hear is the rock thing. All the stations -- AM, most FM stations -- might have one station that has --
